reconcile.note: Keil and Delitzsch argue Jacob's marriage to both sisters predates Sinai, so no law yet existed to violate, since Leviticus 18:18 was legislated only later.

discrepancy.note: Wellhausen treats patriarchal marriage of relations as unrestricted by later Levitical law, a pattern this Jacob-sisters clash instances; Ingersoll presses the specific case.

quotes.text: How did it happen that Jacob, who was in direct communication with God, married, not his deceased wife's sister, but both sisters, while both were living?
quotes.attr: Robert G. Ingersoll (d. 1899), The Christian Religion, pt. III (Reply to Cardinal Gibbons) (1890), on Genesis 29:28.

quotes.text: How did it happen that Jacob, while in direct communication with God, married, not his deceased wife's sister, but both sisters while both were living?
quotes.attr: Robert G. Ingersoll (d. 1899), The Christian Religion, pt. III (1890), "The Wife" dialogue, on Genesis 29:28.

quotes.text: The marriage of relations was by no means prohibited; no offence was taken at the circumstance that Abraham was the husband of his sister (by a different mother).
quotes.attr: Julius Wellhausen (d. 1918), Prolegomena to the History of Israel (1885), on patriarchal-era marriage customs preceding Levitical law.

sides.snippet: Jacob did so, and fulfilled her week. He gave him Rachel his daughter as wife.
sides.verseText: Jacob did so, and fulfilled her week. He gave him Rachel his daughter as wife.

sides.snippet: You shall not take a wife to her sister, to be a rival, to uncover her nakedness, while her sister is yet alive.
